foodKgPerPersonDay.note: Engels app.1: minimum 3 lb (1.36 kg) grain or equivalent per person-day. Roth ch.1: Roman ration ~1.3 kg (850 g grain + ~460 g other), under 1.2 kg with biscuit. High: FM 101-10 (1941) field ration "Average for planning - 6 lbs per ration" (2.7 kg).

waterLPerPersonDay.note: FM 101-10-1/2 (1987) table 2-5 drinking water: temperate 1.5 gal (5.7 L), hot 3.0 gal (11.4 L), cold 2.0 gal. Low: Engels minimum "at least 2 qt." (1.9 L) for marching troops on a grain diet. Drinking only; hygiene/laundry (FM: +5.5 gal) excluded.

fodderKgPerAnimalDay.note: Engels app.1: horse doing moderate work 20-24 lb/day, hard work 24-32 lb (half grain, half fodder); his planning ration 10 lb grain + 10 lb forage = 9.1 kg. High 32 lb = 14.5 kg (FM 101-10 1941: grain 10 lb + hay 14 lb = 10.9 kg). Low: Roth, Wellington's mules 2.3 kg barley + 4.5 kg straw = 6.8 kg.

animalsPer1000.note: Educated guess: porters only; donkeys rare in war before ~3000 BCE.
Educated guess: donkey pack trains and a few carts (tech 1 anchor "donkeys, carts").
Educated guess: chariot armies with 2 horses per chariot plus ox/donkey trains (tech 2 anchor).

Engels table 1: 65,000 personnel with 6,100 cavalry horses + 1,300 baggage + 1,121 provision animals = 131/1000; table 3 arid case with 8,490 provision animals = 245/1000. Engels ch.1: Roman legion ~1 pack animal per 7 combatants (143/1000).
Regional analogy to tech 5 (Louvois 667/1000) for knightly armies with 2-4 horses per man-at-arms; educated guess.
Van Creveld ch.1: typical army of Louvois' day, 60,000 men with 40,000 horses (cavalry, artillery, baggage) = 667/1000.
1812: "over 150,000 horses" for an initial force exceeding 450,000 men = 333/1000. Armee du Nord 1815: 47,000 horses (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horses_in_the_Napoleonic_Wars).
Analogy: horse-drawn divisional trains of 1914 were at least as heavy as the German 1943 infantry division (2,652-6,300 horses per ~17,000 men = 156-370/1000). Grade C.
German 1943 infantry division supply train 2,652 horses, other configurations up to 6,300 (~156-370 per 1000 at ~17,000 men); the US Army in Europe had none ("not a single horse").
Mechanized armies; pack animals only in niche mountain operations.
Mechanized armies; pack animals only in niche mountain operations.

ammoTonsPer1000CombatDay.note: Educated guess: thrown/shot stone and arrows, a few kg per missile-armed man.
Educated guess: javelins, sling stones, arrows.
Educated guess: composite-bow archers on chariots with large arrow loads.
Educated guess: missiles plus torsion-artillery shot; negligible vs food.
Educated guess: longbow/crossbow troops carrying 2-4 kg of missiles each, ~1/4 of the army missile-armed.

Van Creveld ch.1: even in sieges no gun fired more than ~5 rounds/day, Vauban reckoned 4; "consumption of ammunition remained negligible beside that of food and fodder". Musket rounds ~30-40 g incl. powder, 20-40 fired per man.

Van Creveld ch.2: a division of 8,000 carried 147-300 rounds per gun and 60-80 infantry rounds per man; Heilbronn depot 1805 passed 75,000-100,000 rounds/day. ~70 rounds x 35 g/man + ~3 guns/1000 x 100 rounds x 7 kg = ~4.5 t at full expenditure.
Van Creveld ch.4: the 1,000 rounds per barrel stocked in 1914 were almost depleted in 45 days (~22 rounds/gun/day average); Somme 1916: 1.5 million shells for one offensive. Wide range by design.

Offensive division consumed ~750 t/day (~45 kg/man) of all classes; minus FM 101-10 (1941) non-ammunition day of supply 24 lb (10.9 kg) leaves up to ~30 t/1000 at the peak; mid 12 for an ordinary combat day.
FM 101-10-1/2 (1987) table 2-3: Class V 31.29 lb/person/day (14.2 kg) theater average at moderate combat intensity. High ~3x moderate for intense combat (educated guess).
Extrapolated from tech 9 (FM 101-10-1/2 14.2 kg/person moderate) with artillery-heavy 2022-25 practice; educated guess.

supplyTonsPer1000Day.note: Food only: Roth ~1.3 kg/person, Engels 1.36 kg. No animals.
Food 1.36 t + ~50 animals x 9.1 kg; educated guess on animal count.
Food 1.36 t + ~150 animals x 9.1 kg (Engels ration) = 2.7 t.
Engels table 2: 65,000 personnel x 3 lb + ~8,500 animals x 20 lb grain and forage = ~365,000 lb = 166 t/day = 2.55 t/1000 (water excluded).
Food 1.36 t + ~500-600 animals x 9.1 kg; regional analogy to tech 5.
Van Creveld ch.1: 60,000 men eat 120,000 lb bread + 60,000 lb other food; 40,000 horses ~20 lb each = 800,000 lb; total ~980,000 lb = 445 t/day = 7.4 t/1000.
Van Creveld ch.3: German corps 1870 ~100 t/day fodder included (~3.2 t/1000 at ~31,000 men); 1812 Grande Armee 450,000 men x 1.36 kg + 150,000 horses x 9.1 kg = ~4.4 t/1000.
Van Creveld ch.3: II Army 1870 issued food and fodder at 7 lb/man/day (3.2 kg); upper bound FM 101-10 (1941) 24 lb (10.9 kg) classes I-IV. Mid interpolated.

FM 101-10 (1941) par. 83 "Day of supply": 24.0 lb/man/day classes I-IV excl. ammunition (10.9 kg). Low: van Creveld, Barbarossa lorry columns could deliver ~70 t/division/day (~4.2 t/1000, inadequate). High: Red Ball Express 750 t/division offensive (all classes).

FM 101-10-1/2 (1987) table 2-3, lb/person/day: I 4.03, II 3.67, III bulk 53.7, III pkg 0.59, IV 8.5, VI 3.2, VIII 1.22, IX 2.5 = 77.4 lb (35 kg); with class VII end items 15 lb = 92.4 lb (42 kg). Ammunition is separate.
Extrapolated from tech 9 (FM 101-10-1/2, 35 kg/person) with more electronics, drones and fuel; educated guess.

fuelTonsPerVehicleDay.note: Per combat vehicle that moves or fights. M1: 1.5-3 US gal per mile; 50-100 km/day = 47-186 gal (0.15-0.57 t) plus turbine idling. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_Sherman: M4A2 214-470 L/100 km (0.09-0.4 t for 50-100 km). Truck fuel is in supplyTonsPer1000Day (class III).

carryKgPerSoldier.note: Engels ch.1: a man can carry about 80 lb (36 kg) for extended distances. Roth ch.2: legionary burden 24.6 kg without rations (low); with 17 days' rations 43.4 kg, shown plausible by Junkelmann's experiment (high).

carryKgPerPackAnimal.note: Engels ch.1: horse or mule ~200 lb (91 kg), camel 300 lb (136 kg); planning average 250 lb (113 kg). Roth: camel load 175 kg (high).

carryKgPerWagon.note: Roth ch.4: Theodosian Code limit 1,075 Roman lb (352 kg); Diocletian's edict 393 kg; Bachrach: two-wheeled cart 500 kg, four-wheeled 650 kg ("most reasonable"). High: van Creveld, four-horse wagon c.1805 "around one ton".

carriedDaysFood.note: Educated guess: what a warrior band carries on the back.
Educated guess: back loads plus donkeys.
Educated guess: back loads plus ox/donkey trains.

Roth ch.2: Josephus, 3 days' rations per legionary; Historia Augusta and Ammianus, 17 days (18.8 kg); contubernium with mules 5 + 11-13 days. Engels: Macedonians carrying 30 lb could hold ~10 days of grain.
Educated guess: medieval armies relied on forage and baggage carts.
Van Creveld ch.1-2: 18th-c. bread wagons covered a few days ("five days' system"); 1805 plan: wagons for 116,000 men for 11 days.
Van Creveld ch.2: 1805 transport plan, wagons to carry provisions for 116,000 men for eleven days (high); only part of it materialised.
Van Creveld ch.3: II Army 1870 took 4,750 t of food and fodder, "suffice to supply 100,000 men for 17 days" (high). Mid: organic trains of ~6 days.

Rations held inside the division, 1941-45. US 2 (FM 101-10 1941 par. 78). Japan 5 (TM-E 30-480: 2 on the man, 1 unit train, 2 division transport; 3-10 ordered per operation). Germany 6.5 (TM-E 30-451 VI: 4 full + 2.5 iron rations; about 10 in the army). USSR 8 (TM 30-430 Fig. 16: regiment 3 days + division 5 days). Median 5.75. High 10: Japanese operations and German army-level reserve.
Educated guess: 3 days of MREs per soldier plus brigade stocks.

water.note: No land forage on water cells.

plains.note: Perjes rule (cited in Roth ch.4): an area can feed an army 3-4x its own population for a few days. Mixed farmland/pasture at ~5-15 persons/km2 x 3.5 = 15-50. Educated guess on density.

cropland.note: Roth ch.4 citing Perjes: armies could live off the land only above ~35 persons/km2 (19th c.) or ~18/km2 (van Creveld) moving; an area supplies 3-4x its population for a few days -> 18-40 x 3.5 = 60-140 person-days/km2/day. Cross-check Engels: 160 t grain per sq mi per year (two-field) = ~124 person-days/km2/day gross.

forest.note: Educated guess: sparse settlement (~2-5/km2) x Perjes 3.5 multiplier.

hills.note: Educated guess: terraced/pastoral land ~5-15 persons/km2 x 3.5.

mountains.note: Educated guess: valley settlement ~1-5 persons/km2 x 3.5.

desert.note: Educated guess: oases only; Engels' Gedrosian march shows the army starving.

steppe.note: Educated guess: pastoral herds at ~1-3 persons/km2 x 3.5; nomad armies feed from own herds.

wetland.note: Educated guess: low settlement density, fish and fowl.

urban.note: Educated guess: town granaries and markets; a 0.25 deg urban cell averages far above the 35/km2 Perjes threshold.

forageWinterFactor.note: Roth ch.4: lack of fodder in winter made it necessary to go into winter quarters; van Creveld: campaigns normally started in April when 6 months of stored flour were on hand. Stored grain remains, green fodder does not. Magnitude is an educated guess.

forageDepletion.note: Fraction of the remaining forage removed per day of occupation. Perjes (via Roth ch.4): an area feeds 3-4x its population only "for a few days" -> exhausted in ~3-5 days (0.2-0.35/day). Engels: Alexander could not retreat by the same route since the crops were eaten.

forageDependence.note: Educated guess: depots appear (tech 2 anchor "ox wagons, depots").
Roth ch.4-6: Roman armies combined supply lines (waterborne, overland) with organized foraging and requisition; Engels: Alexander depended on local purchase and fleet supply.
Educated guess: medieval armies lived largely off the land.
Van Creveld ch.1: 18th-c. armies "lived off the country as a matter of course"; magazines could carry little more than ten per cent of requirements.
Van Creveld ch.2: Napoleon's armies lived mainly by requisition, supplemented by magazines and wagon trains.
Van Creveld ch.3: in 1870-1 the Germans were "compelled ... to live off the country much as Napoleon's soldiers had done"; by 1914 ammunition and much food came by rail.
Van Creveld ch.5-7: WWII armies were rail/truck supplied; Germans still requisitioned food in the East. FM 101-10 (1941) day of supply assumes depot feeding.

throughputRoadTonsDay.note: Educated guess: porter columns, each carrying ~25 kg and eating part of it.
Educated guess: donkey trains at ~90 kg per animal.
Educated guess: ox carts and pack trains.
Roth: wagon 500-650 kg; ~150-300 wagon-loads/day on an engineered road; educated guess.
Educated guess: carts on poor roads, river transport separate.
Educated guess: comparable to tech 6 wagon services.
Van Creveld ch.2: 1805 Strasbourg-Augsburg service of 17 sections x 60 four-horse wagons "must have amounted to between sixty and 120 tons per day".
Educated guess: horse-drawn columns plus first lorries.
Red Ball Express peak 5,958 vehicles, ~12,500 t/day (a dedicated two-road network). Low (single road without a convoy system) and mid are educated composites.
Educated guess: modern truck fleets on a main supply route.
Educated guess: as tech 9 with palletised loading.

throughputRailTonsDay.note: Van Creveld ch.4: single line 8 trains/day in 1870, 40 by 1914; double line 12 -> 60. FM 101-10 (1941): single track two-way 20 trains per direction, double track 60. Van Creveld ch.5: 1941 supply trains of 450 t. 8 x 450 = 3,600; 20 x 450 = 9,000; 60 x 450 = 27,000.

Educated guess: medieval harbour with cogs.
Educated guess: steam-era quays and cranes.
Van Creveld: Tobruk theoretically 1,500 t/day but "rarely exceeded 600"; Cherbourg scheduled 6,000 t/day; British ports 17,000 t/day before Antwerp.
